Cache Lab

A real particle pool: 32 bytes per particle, updated every frame. Same particles, same code. Only the order of the reads changes. Watch what that does to the time.

Rain and blood particles, night city level. Goal: 500,000 particles, at least 10 seconds played, and the loop still reads memory in order.

    Order test
    
      
    
    
    
    The same update loop, time frozen, at four sizes. Each size runs twice: reads in slot order, and reads in a fully shuffled order. It takes about 10 seconds; the live view pauses while it runs. Watch the last column jump once the data no longer fits in your CPU's caches.
    
    
    Not run yet.

    What this shows
    
    
    
      
    Order is a cost
    The same 500,000 updates take several times longer when each read jumps somewhere new. Nothing in the code got slower. The memory did.
    
      
    Size decides how much
    When the data fits in the caches (20K particles is 640 KB), a shuffled order costs little. When it doesn't fit, every jump is a trip to RAM.
    
      
    Containers decide order
    A free list scrambles the order on its own within seconds. Swap-and-pop keeps the live particles packed, so the loop always reads front to back.
    
    
    
    
    Measured live with performance.now(): this is the real loop, in JavaScript, on your device. A particle is 8 floats (32 bytes) in one big Float32Array. The "Skip 10 s" button fast-forwards the deaths and births of particles without timing them; it scrambles the free list the same way as letting time run. A C++ or Burst build would be faster overall, and your CPU's cache sizes decide where the jump happens, but the ratio is the lesson.
